Plans for Evaluating Structured Generative Search Summaries

Conference: arxiv; May 2026; version 1
Tetsuya Sakai email: tetsuyasakai@acm.org Affiliation: Waseda University/Naver Corporation, Tokyo, Japan , Jina Lee email: jinalee1697@ruri.waseda.jp Affiliation: Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan , Hanpei Fang email: hanpeifang@ruri.waseda.jp Affiliation: Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan and Young-In Song email: song.youngin@navercorp.com Affiliation: Naver Corporation, Seongnam, Korea
© none
Abstract.

We propose a framework for evaluating structured generative search summaries that are placed atop organic web search results. A structured summary, generated by a large language model, typically consists of an overview, several sections with section titles, and a list of source documents that are cited within the summary. We then describe our plans for implementing and evaluating the framework.

Keywords: 
evaluation measures, large language models, summaries, web search

1. Introduction

The advance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is rapidly changing the experience of web search engine users. To try to quickly satisfy the user’s information need without making them read retrieved web pages, search engine companies have started to include a generated output in the Search Engine Result Page (SERP) for some queries, atop traditional “organic” web search results. Figure 1 shows a typical structure of a generated output that comprises a structured summary and a doclist (i.e., a list of cited documents). Unlike plain-text search engine outputs that have been considered in earlier studies (e.g., (Sakai et al., 2011)), the structured summary starts with a short textual overview that is designed to address the user’s query directly, followed by one or more textual sections, where each section consists of a section heading that briefly describes what the section is about, and a section body that contains one or more statements. In general, the overview and each statement are accompanied by zero or more citation numbers. Each citation number points to one of the documents in the doclist shown beneath the structured summary. Thus the doclist is a short list of cited web pages, typically representing a subset of the traditional organic web search results that are placed below it.

For over two decades, search engine companies have used nDCG and nDCG-like measures to evaluate and optimise document lists: see, for example, Burges et al. (2005). However, as generated outputs in SERPs like the one illustrated in Figure 1 are becoming more common than ever, we need a sound framework to evaluate such outputs. In light of this situation, the present study addresses the question of evaluating the structured summary part of a SERP, i.e., the red parts shown in Figure 1, by treating the doclist as a given. Put another way, our concern is: Given this doclist, how good is this structured summary? Which parts of it are good/bad and why? How can we improve it? This evaluation problem is particularly important because LLMs are known to “hallucinate” (Kalai et al., 2025)11 1 We have no intention of anthropomorphising LLMs (Förster and Skop, 2026): hence the quotation marks. even if the source documents are accurate, misinformation can be injected at the text generation step, which may have a substantial negative impact on the user. That is, not only relevance to the information need but also faithfulness (Cao and Wang, 2024; Es et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2023; Lamsiyah et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023; Rashkin et al., 2023; van Dort and Heuss, 2026; Zhou et al., 2023) to the source documents should be considered. Moreover, for some types of queries, evaluating the comprehensiveness of the structured summary will be needed: for example, we would like to be able to ask: For this query, do these sections of this structured summary cover all aspects that should be covered? Evaluating the relevance and faithfulness of parts of the structured summary is closely related to the traditional notion of precision, which requires systems to reduce noise in the search results; Evaluating the comprehensiveness of the entire structured summary is closely related to the traditional notion of recall, which requires systems to prevent missing information that should not be missed.

In this paper, we propose a framework for evaluating structured generative search summaries that are placed atop organic web search results, like the one shown in Figure 1. We then describe our plans for implementing and evaluating the framework. The outcomes of our implementation and evaluation will be reported elsewhere.

2. Related Work

2.1. Summarisation and Complex Question Answering Evaluation

Historically, text summarisation and question answering tasks had a few aspects in common regarding how the systems’ textual responses were evaluated. Firstly, it was assumed that the ground truth data (i.e., manually-composed reference summaries or manually-identified correct answers) were available. Second, the comparison of the system response and the ground truth were performed by decomposing both into smaller units such as N-grams (Lin, 2004), semantic content units (Nenkova et al., 2007), or nuggets (Dang et al., 2007; Mitamura et al., 2010; Rajput et al., 2011; Voorhees, 2004). Among the nugget-based approaches, our work is inspired by the S-measure/U-measure frameworks (Sakai et al., 2011; Sakai and Dou, 2013), which are unique in that they take into account the position of each nugget within the summary for the evaluation.

The modern challenge in evaluating system-generated texts, however, is that we often do not have access to the ground truth; it may not even exist. This is also the case in our study, where the task is to evaluate generated summaries for any web search query entered by the users. Thus we need a reference-free (Es et al., 2024; Joko and Hasibi, 2026) evaluation approach.

2.2. RAG and Conversational Search Evaluation

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) combines the strengths of IR and the generation capability of LLMs (Lewis et al., 2020; Petroni et al., 2024). As LLMs can now extract nuggets from text with reasonable accuracy, Pradeep et al. (2025) “refactored” the nugget-based evaluation method from the TREC 2003 question answering track (Lin, 2004) for the TREC 2024 RAG track; see also Alaofi et al. (2024); Łajewska and Balog (2025). Nugget-based and similar RAG evaluation methods were also adopted at the TREC iKAT 2024 track (Abbasiantaeb et al., 2025) and the TREC 2024 NeuCLIR track (Samarinas et al., 2025). Other nugget-based RAG evaluation efforts include the ongoing NTCIR-19 R2C2 task (Sakai et al., 2025b).

Conversational search (Radlinski and Craswell, 2017) (or Conversational Information Access (Joko and Hasibi, 2026)) generally involves multi-turn system responses. (See also pre-LLM-era efforts in interactive question answering (Dang et al., 2007).) The present study focusses on single-turn responses, i.e., a single generated summary for a given query. However, our work builds on a user model proposed in the context of conversational search, namely, that described in Sakai et al. (2025c). In their conversational search user model, a population of users with the same information need examines a ranked list of nuggets, which represent parts of the system responses (which can be multi-turn), from top to bottom. Some of the users abandon the list after seeing a particular relevant nugget; others continue on.22 2 The user model is similar to that of the Sakai/Robertson Normalised Cumulative Utility (NCU) measures (Sakai and Robertson, 2008); the main difference is that the NCU user model is for ranked list of documents such as web pages. Instead of using nuggets as the basic evaluation unit, we leverage the structured nature of our generated summaries, and use “line numbers” in the summary as the basic unit, as we shall describe in Section 3.1. Inspired by the aforementioned S-measure/U-measure approach, we use line numbers as the positions of relevant pieces of information within the summary.

2.3. Evaluation Axes

The SWAN (Schematised Weighted Average Nugget) framework (Sakai, 2023) lists 21 evaluation criteria for conversational systems, including groundedness (i.e., Is the claim supported by a piece of evidence?) (Menick et al., 2022), sufficiency (i.e., Does the system’s turn satisfy the requests in the previous user turn?) modesty (i.e., Is the system’s answer confidence score appropriate?) (Sakai, 2024; Sakai et al., 2025b), fair exposure (i.e., Does the system mention entities from different groups fairly in its responses?) (Sakai et al., 2025c), and harmlessness (i.e., “no stereotypes, no microaggressions, no threats, no sexual aggression, no insults, no hate or harassment” (Glaese et al., 2022)). See also the HHH (helpful, honest, and harmless) criteria of Askell et al. (2021).

Joko and Hasibi (2026) take an approach related to SWAN for evaluating conversational information access, where not only turn-level axes such as interestingness (i.e., engagingness of SWAN) but also dialogue-level axes such as task completion and overall impression are considered. The Dialogue Quality subtasks of the NTCIR DialEval tasks (Tao and Sakai, 2022; Zeng et al., 2020) also used related criteria, including task accomplishment and customer satisfaction, in the context of evaluating helpdesk-customer (human-human) dialogues.

In terms of evaluation criteria, our framework concerns relevance to the user’s turn, faithfulness (Cao and Wang, 2024; Es et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2023; Lamsiyah et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023; Rashkin et al., 2023; van Dort and Heuss, 2026; Zhou et al., 2023) with respect to the cited documents (which we equate with groundedness),33 3 Rashkin et al. (2023) define a related concept called attribution. Also, while Wallat et al. (2025) define citation faithfulness based on whether the model actually relies on cited documents rather than post-rationalising the citations, this is out of the scope of this present study as our evaluation concerns how the summaries look like from the user’s viewpoint. and comprehensiveness which is similar to sufficiency (Sakai, 2023) and coverage (Gienapp et al., 2024). While it is relatively easy to discuss the relevance and faithfulness of a given summary, that is not the case with comprehensiveness, since we generally lack the ground truth and therefore there is no notion of recall base. Hence, to define comprehensiveness, we require multiple summaries per user query, so that a concept akin to relative recall (Clarke and Willet, 1997) can be leveraged. We shall define comprehensiveness in Section 3.4.

2.4. Reading Models

The SIGIR 2024 perspectives paper by Gienapp et al. (2024) has a movitation similar to ours except that they do not discuss the structured nature of generated summaries for a given query. They propose a user reading model which is a “monotonically decreasing weight function over statements that discounts the contribution of later statements in a response” to reward “putting the most important pieces of information first.” This is exactly what the aforementioned S-measure from 2011 (Sakai et al., 2011) featured. In this paper, we also employ a user reading model, but ours is based on the assumption that there is a population of users reading a structured summary, as mentioned in Section 2.2.

2.5. LLMs Evaluating LLMs

There is a controversy regarding the evaluation of LLMs using LLMs (Clarke and Dietz, 2025; Faggioli et al., 2023; Panickssery et al., 2024; Sakai et al., 2025a; Soboroff, 2025; Upadhyay et al., 2024). In the context of web search, clearly our goal is to satisfy the user, not an LLM. However, our view is that LLMs can be leveraged effectively when used within a divide and conquer evaluation approach: “if LLMs’ behaviours are not altogether predictable, then we should try to reduce the number of confounding uncertainty factors, by giving them simple and controllable subtasks instead of a complex task” (Sakai et al., 2025b). Thus, whenever we require labellers, we hire either humans or LLMs while ensuring that the labelling tasks are relatively straightforward.

3. Proposed Evaluation Framework

Unlike existing studies that explore the evaluation of “flat” text with citations (e.g. (Gienapp et al., 2024)), our evaluation framework evaluates the structured summary part of a SERP in the context of a given query and a doclist, as illustrated in Figure 1. The structured summary generally consists of an overview oo followed by I(≥0)I(\geq 0) sections, where each section seci\textit{sec}_{i} (i=1,…,Ii=1,\ldots,I) contains a section heading hih_{i} and Ji(>0)J_{i}(>0) statements si​j​(j=1,…,Ji)s_{ij}(j=1,\ldots,J_{i}). The overview and the statements are accompanied by zero or more citation numbers. (Instead of an overview at the beginning of the structured summary, a short “summary” may be placed at the end: our evaluation framework accommodates both. Hereafter, we shall focus on structured summaries with an initial overview.)

Sections 3.1-3.3 describe our Expected User Experience (XUX) measure, which evaluates a given structured summary from a user perspective. However, as XUX cannot quantify neither “relevant information that is missing in the text” nor “balanced coverage of multiple aspects relevant to the information need,” Section 3.4 describes our Comprehensiveness (Comp) measure which is designed to address these questions by “pooling” sections from multiple structured summaries; this is similar in spirit to estimating the recall of multiple “10-blue-links” search engines (Clarke and Willet, 1997) and to the traditional document pooling for constructing IR test collections (Sparck Jones and Rijsbergen, 1975; Sakai, 2019; Voorhees and Harman, 2005). Finally, Section 3.5 defines our quick summary measure, SGSS (Structured Generative Search Summary) score, as a combination of XUX and Comp.

3.1. Expected User Experience

For a given query and a structured summary SS, we envision a population of users each having an information need represented by that query. We assume that users generally read SS starting from the top, and that different users abandon (i.e., give up reading) SS at different positions within SS.44 4 This linear reading behaviour assumption is analogous to the linear traversal assumption behind traditional IR evaluation measures. To define an Abandonment Probability Distribution (APD) for the user population over different positions within SS, let us first define line numbers within SS, where the overview (oo), section headings (hih_{i}’s), and statements (si​js_{ij}’s) each constitute one line. Then, the total number of lines in SS is given by

(1) L=1+I+∑i=1IJi,L=1+I+\sum_{i=1}^{I}J_{i}\ ,

as depicted in the right part of Figure 2.

In ranked list evaluation in IR, we often apply a document cutoff dd to SERPs and consider only the top dd documents. Similarly, let us introduce LmaxL_{\mathrm{max}}, the maximum number of lines in a structured summary any user is expected to read. In effect, this truncates the structured summary to only top LmaxL_{\mathrm{max}} lines in order to penalise excessively long texts. (If the truncation is unnecessary, let Lmax=∞L_{\mathrm{max}}=\infty.) Let L′=min⁡(L,Lmax)L^{\prime}=\min(L,L_{\mathrm{max}}). As a simple instantiation of the APD, we consider a uniform distribution over L′L^{\prime}, as depicted in the left part of Figure 2. That is, we assume that the users are equally likely to stop reading at any line at or above Line L′L^{\prime}, due to satisfaction or dissatisfaction or for some other reason. This generalises the uniform distribution over relevant documents used in Average Precision and Q, as described in the aforementioned Sakai/Robertson NCU suite of IR measures (Sakai and Robertson, 2008).

One way to determine LmaxL_{\mathrm{max}} would be to observe real user behaviour data over the summaries, such as clicks, scrolls, and hovers with timestamps. Another approach would be to follow the S-measure approach (Sakai et al., 2011), where it is assumed that the users’ reading speed is constant, and that the user has a MM-minute window to satisfy their need. For example, from Rhiu et al. (2017, p.206), we can assume that the typical reading speed for Korean texts is about 500 characters per minute; hence we can assume that the user will read up to 500​M500M characters; if the average character length per line in a Korean summary is avlen, we can let Lmax≈500​M/avlenL_{\mathrm{max}}\approx 500M/\textit{avlen}.

Having defined the probability that users will abandon the structured summary at Line ll, let us now consider the quality of the summary from the viewpoint of these different users. More specifically, for the group of users who abandon the summary after reading Line ll, let X⁡(l)X(l) denote their overall user experience, which we shall instantiate in the following sections. Then, we can compute Expected User Experience (XUX) as an expectation of X⁡(l)X(l) over the aforementioned uniform probability distribution.

(2) XUX=1L′​∑l=1L′X⁡(l).\textit{XUX}=\frac{1}{L^{\prime}}\sum_{l=1}^{L^{\prime}}X(l)\ .

We can also consider a simplified variant of XUX with a modified APD, by assuming that users will abandon the structured summary only after reading the overview line or after reading an entire section. Let F⁡(l)F(l) be one if line ll is either an overview line or the Final line of a section, and zero otherwise. Again, by assuming a uniform probability mass function over the lines where F⁡(l)=1F(l)=1, we can define:

(3) XUXF=11+I​∑l=1L′F⁡(I)​X​(l).\textit{XUX}_{F}=\frac{1}{1+I}\sum_{l=1}^{L^{\prime}}F(I)X(l)\ .

Note that, for simplicity, XUXF does not consider LmaxL_{\mathrm{max}}.

Clearly, XUX score can also be Generalised so that we can employ any valid APD over the line numbers:

(4) XUXG=∑lPr​(l)​X​(l),\textit{XUX}_{G}=\sum_{l}\textit{Pr}(l)X(l)\ ,

where Pr​(l)\textit{Pr}(l) is the probability that the users of a given query will abandon the summary at Line ll, such that ∑l=1L′Pr​(l)=1\sum_{l=1}^{L^{\prime}}\textit{Pr}(l)=1. Considering non-uniform APDs for Pr​(l)\textit{Pr}(l) will be left for future work; however, our view is that evaluation measures should be as simple and interpretable as possible.

3.2. User Experience Building Blocks

Given a single structured summary SS like the one shown in Figure 1, we quantify the user experience X⁡(l)X(l) for each line ll of SS as described below. Hereafter, we shall refer to labellers for defining the building blocks for X⁡(l)X(l): they can be human, an LLM, or a combination of the two.

3.2.1. Overview Quality

The overview part of the structured summary is generally short, and is accompanied by zero or more citations. We let labellers rate the overview quality using the following criteria, where each criterion is on a 3-point scale (Perfectly/Partially/No).

Overview Sufficiency (OS):

Does the overview satisfy the information need behind the query?

Overview Faithfulness (OF):

Do the cited documents (when taken together) entail the overview’s claims?

Overview Representativeness (OR):

Does the overview actually serve as a good overview of the sections?

Thus, OS, OF, and OR are about the query-overview relationship, the overview-doclist relationship, and the overview-sections relationship, respectively. We then map the labels to scores in the 0-1 range.

For overview oo, let OS​(o),OF​(o),OR​(o)\textit{OS}(o),\textit{OF}(o),\textit{OR}(o) denote their OS, OF, and OR scores. The overview quality of oo can be expressed as:

(5) OQ​(o)=wOS​OS​(o)+wOF​OF​(o)+wOR​OR​(o),\textit{OQ}(o)=w_{\mathrm{OS}}\textit{OS}(o)+w_{\mathrm{OF}}\textit{OF}(o)+w_{\mathrm{OR}}\textit{OR}(o)\ ,

where wOS,wOF,wORw_{\mathrm{OS}},w_{\mathrm{OF}},w_{\mathrm{OR}} are weights, which we shall discuss later.

Note that relevance is a necessary but not sufficient condition for sufficiency: we ask whether the overview satisfies the information need. As described in Section 3.2.3, we quantify relevance at the statement level.

3.2.2. Heading Quality

As each section contains one section heading and one or more statements, we quantify the quality of each heading in terms of Heading Representativeness (HR) as follows. For the jj-th statement (j≤Jij\leq J_{i}) of the ii-th section (i≤Ii\leq I), we obtain a relevance grade rel​(hi,si​j)\textit{rel}(h_{i},s_{ij}) by asking the labellers how relevant the statement is to the section heading on a 3-point scale (Perfectly/Partially/Not relevant). We then map the labels to graded relevance values g⁡(hi,si​j)g(h_{i},s_{ij}) in the 0-1 range and finally compute the average relevance of the statements to the section heading.

(6) HR​(hi)=∑jg⁡(hi,si​j)Ji.\textit{HR}(h_{i})=\frac{\sum_{j}g(h_{i},s_{ij})}{J_{i}}.\

Thus, HR is about the heading-statement relationship.

3.2.3. Statement Quality

We label each statement in each section using the following criteria, where each criterion is on a 3-point scale (Perfectly/Partially/No).

Statement Relevance (SRel):

Is the statement relevant to the information need behind the query?

Statement Faithfulness (SF):

Do the cited documents (when taken together) entail the statement?

Thus, SRel is about the query-statement relationship, while SF is about the statement-doclist relationship. We then map the labels to scores in the 0-1 range; for statement si​js_{ij}. We denote the SRel and SR scores of statement si​js_{ij} by SRel​(si​j),SF​(si​j)\textit{SRel}(s_{ij}),\textit{SF}(s_{ij}).

3.3. Top-heavy XUX Instantiations

Let cc be a component of a given structured summary, which can be an overview, a section heading, or a statement. Let line​(c)\textit{line}(c) denote the line number of component cc. We instantiate the XUX formula (Eq. 2) with

(7) X⁡(l)=X′​(l)l,X(l)=\frac{X^{\prime}(l)}{l}\ ,
X′​(l)=OQ​(o)+wHR​∑i,line​(hi)≤lHR​(hi)X^{\prime}(l)=\textit{OQ}(o)+w_{\mathrm{HR}}\sum_{i,\,\textit{line}(h_{i})\leq l}\textit{HR}(h_{i})
(8) +wSRel∑i,j,line​(si​j)≤lSRel(si​j)+wSF∑i,j,line​(si​j)≤lSF(si​j),+w_{\mathrm{SRel}}\sum_{i,j,\ \textit{line}(s_{ij})\leq l}\textit{SRel}(s_{ij})+w_{\mathrm{SF}}\sum_{i,j,\ \textit{line}(s_{ij})\leq l}\textit{SF}(s_{ij})\ ,

where the w∙w_{\bullet}’s are weights associated with each component.55 5 Eqs. 5 and 8, when taken together, do not guarantee X⁡(l)≤lX(l)\leq l unless wOS+wOF+wOR≤1w_{\mathrm{OS}}+w_{\mathrm{OF}}+w_{\mathrm{OR}}\leq 1 and wHR≤1w_{\mathrm{HR}}\leq 1 and wSRel+wSF≤1w_{\mathrm{SRel}}+w_{\mathrm{SF}}\leq 1, so that each line contributes a total score no larger than 1 to X′​(l)X^{\prime}(l). Hence, without these constraints, XUX (Eq. 2) may potentially attain a value higher than 1. We do not impose these constraints unless a strictly normalised measure is necessary. We shall briefly describe one method for setting these weights in Section 4.

It is important to note that Eq. 7 makes XUX top-heavy, just as the use of precision makes average precision top heavy (Robertson, 2008) (and the use of the blended ratio makes Q-measure top heavy (Sakai, 2014)). That is, this instantiation rewards early presentation of good content. To see why, let us take the structured summaries illustrated in Figure 3 as examples, where, for simplicity, each text contains three sections, each with only one statement, and wOS=wHRep=wSR=1,wOF=wOR=wSF=0w_{\mathrm{OS}}=w_{\mathrm{HRep}}=w_{\mathrm{SR}}=1,w_{\mathrm{OF}}=w_{\mathrm{OR}}=w_{\mathrm{SF}}=0. That is, we ignore OF, OR, and SF scores for now. Furthermore, suppose that the OS, HRep and SR scores are simply either 1 or 0 as indicated in the figure. The only essential difference between texts (a) and (b) is the ordering of the three sections, where exactly one of these sections was given zero scores. The figure shows how user experience X⁡(l)X(l) is calcuated at each line ll; it can be observed that the sum of X⁡(l)X(l) is higher for (a) than that for (b). The top heaviness is achieved by (i) the denominator ll of X⁡(l)X(l), which discounts the user experience if a good content moves to a later line in the text; and (ii) the numerator X′​(l)X^{\prime}(l) (Eq. 8) which ensures that a good content at Line ll contributes also to Line (l+1)(l+1) and below.

3.4. Comprehensiveness

In 1973, Cooper, in the context of discussing the choice of IR evaluation measures, remarked: “Why should the status of documents which the system user has not examined have any influence on a user-oriented performance rating?” (Cooper, 1973, p.95). (See also Zobel et al. (2009) from 2009.) The XUX measure discussed above aligns with the above “precision-oriented” perspective since it only evaluates a given structured summary, i.e., what the user actually sees. However, from a system developer (e.g., search engine company) point of view, we would also like to ask “What is missing in the structured summary? What else could we have offered to the user?”: a “recall-oriented” perspective.

As we have discussed in Section 2.3, we are dealing with reference-free evaluation and therefore we have to establish a notion similar to relative recall. In order to do this, we require that we have multiple summaries for a given query so that we can “pool” information contributed by each of them. More specifically, as we are evaluating structured summaries, we pool sections from multiple structured summaries to compare them in terms of comprehensiveness as described below. As each section can be regarded as a representation of an aspect or perspective relevant to the information need, comprehensiveness evaluation asks “how many of available relevant aspects are covered by this particular structured summary?” Here, note that a section from Summary aa and one from Summary bb may not be identical and yet represent the same aspect; a section from Summary aa may even be roughly equivalent to multiple sections from Summary bb. Thus, the situation is much more complicated than traditional document pooling that merely involves merging document IDs or the task of identifying near-duplicate passages (or passage equivalence classes) (Craswell et al., 2024). Our approach is designed to address these issues.

Given N(>1)N(>1) structured summaries S1,…,SNS^{1},\ldots,S^{N} for the same query qq, we first pool the sections. Let secin\textit{sec}^{n}_{i} denote the ii-th section of Summary SnS^{n} which contains InI^{n} sections (i=1,…,Ini=1,\ldots,I^{n}). For comprehensiveness evaluation, we require that each summary contains at least one section (In>1I^{n}>1). The pool PP for qq is defined as

(9) P=⋃n=1N⋃i=1In{secin}.P=\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}\bigcup_{i=1}^{I^{n}}\{\textit{sec}^{n}_{i}\}\ .

For example, in Figure 4 (where N=2N=2), Summary aa contributes sections a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} to the pool, while Summary bb contributes section b1b_{1} to the pool.

Let K=|P|K=|P|, and let seck∗\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k} denote the kk-th pooled section in PP (k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K). Note that K≥NK\geq N as we assume that each summary contributes at least one section. For each summary SnS^{n} and each seck∗\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k}, we define a 3-point relevance label (Perfectly/Partially/Not relevant) rel​(Sn,seck∗)\textit{rel}(S^{n},\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k}) as follows.

If seck∗\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k} is a section from SnS^{n} then rel​(Sn,seck∗)=Perfectly relevant\textit{rel}(S^{n},\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k})=\textit{Perfectly relevant}
else rel​(Sn,seck∗)=\textit{rel}(S^{n},\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k})= label obtained by asking labellers how
relevant SnS^{n} is to seck∗\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k} (even though seck∗\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k} is not a section of SnS^{n}).

For example, in Figure 4 (where K=3K=3), Summary aa is labelled as partially relevant to Section b1b_{1}; on the other hand, Summary bb is labelled as not relevant to Section a1a_{1} but partially relevant to a2a_{2}. In this way, each summary is compared with each section from a different summary.

Next, we map the labels rel​(Sn,seck∗)\textit{rel}(S^{n},\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k}) to graded relevance scores g⁡(Sn,seck∗)g(S^{n},\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k}), and further compute:

(10) g′​(Sn,seck=1∗)=g⁡(Sn,seck∗)∑k=1Kg⁡(Sn,seck∗)g^{\prime}(S^{n},\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k=1})=\frac{g(S^{n},\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k})}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}g(S^{n},\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k})}

so that ∑k=1Kg′​(Sn,seck∗)=1\sum_{k=1}^{K}g^{\prime}(S^{n},\textit{sec}^{\ast}_{k})=1. Thus we obtain a probability mass function FnF^{n} over the pooled sections. Examples are given at the bottom of Figure 4.

Let us assume that the pooled sections are equally important (just as the TREC Web Tracks (2009-2012) assumed that the subtopics of a given topic are equally important for search result diversification (Clarke et al., 2013)). Accordingly, we employ a uniform distribution UU over the pooled sections as our gold (i.e., target) distribution, with probability 1/K1/K for each pooled section. The comprehensiveness of SnS^{n} can then be defined as

(11) Comp​(Sn)=1−JSD​(Fn,U),\textit{Comp}(S^{n})=1-\textit{JSD}(F^{n},U)\ ,

where JSD​(∙,∙)\textit{JSD}(\bullet,\bullet) denotes the Jensen-Shannon Divergence between two probability mass functions (Ekstrand et al., 2022; Sakai et al., 2023). Note that Comp measures the similarity between FnF^{n} and UU. For example, consider a simple situation where there are only two pooled sections, each representing two contrasting viewpoints for a particular topic addressed in the query. The above Comp score will reward a structured summary that covers both viewpoints in a balanced manner. For the examples in Figure 4, the Comp scores for aa and bb would be 0.983 and 0.792, respectively, and therefore aa is considered more comprehensive.

3.5. SGSS

To compare multiple structured summaries for a given query, plotting XUX scores against the corresponding Comp scores may be useful. In addition, as a quick summary measure, the two can be combined to form an overall Structured Generated Search Summary (SGSS) score.

(12) SGSS​(S)=XUX​(S)+wComp​Comp​(S),\textit{SGSS}(S)=\textit{XUX}(S)+w_{\mathrm{Comp}}\textit{Comp}(S)\ ,

where wcompw_{\mathrm{comp}} is a weight that determines the impact of Comp relative to the weights defined in Eq. 8.

4. Plans

We are currently preparing data for implementing and evaluating the SGSS evaluation framework described above. Below, we describe our ongoing work and near-future plans.

4.1. Dataset Construction

We are collecting generated output data (See Figure 1) for real search engine queries. As comprehensiveness evaluation requires multiple structured summaries per query, we will collect at least two (each with one or more sections) structured summaries per query by using multiple generative summarisers. Moreover, from these structured summaries, we will automatically create degraded versions of the summaries using strategies such as the following:

NoHeadings:

Remove all section headings from the original summary. Comparing the original summary with a NoHeadings version in terms of SGSS should be able to tell us the importance of the section headings. Note that NoHeadings summaries will receive zero HR scores (Eq. 6).

NoSection1:

Remove the first section from the original summary. As the first section of a structured summary is generally expected to be at least as important as the other sections, if we compare the original summary with its NoSection1 version, we expect SGSS to generally prefer the original over the NoSection1 version (unless the quality of the first section is low).

We will construct summary pair data for a query set, where the two structured summaries represent two different generative summarisers. To have human labellers compare the two summaries side by side, we will develop an annotation interface similar to that for comparing traditional ten-blue-links (e.g. (Sakai and Zeng, 2021, Figure 1)). We will assign H(>2)H(>2) human labellers to each summary pair, and each human labeller will provide the following labels.

  • •

    OS (Overview Sufficiency), OF (Overview Faithfulness), and OR (Overview Representativeness) labels for the overviews of the two summaries (3-point scale);

  • •

    An HR (Heading Representativeness) label for each heading of the two summaries (3-point scale);

  • •

    SRel (Statement Relevance) and SF (Statement Faithfulness) labels for each statement of the two summaries (3-point scale);

  • •

    An absolute Comprehensiveness label for each summary (3-point scale);

  • •

    A preference label which declares which of the two summaries is preferred (LEFT or RIGHT).

In addition, we will have LLMs provide the same set of labels. We can then average the labels over the (human or combined) labellers. In addition, we can derive similar data for the degraded summaries: we assume that an original summary is preferred over its NoHeadings or NoSection1 version (if the removed section contained at least one relevant statement); the other absolute labels for the original summary mentioned above can simply be inherited to its degraded version.

The dataset thus constructed will be split into a training part and a test part: the former will be utilised for tuning purposes, i.e., for setting the weights, and the latter will be used for evaluating and validating the SGSS framework.

Besides the above dataset, we will utilise a commercial search engine query log to explore methods for estimating the maximum time the user spends on a structured summary, to determine LmaxL_{\mathrm{max}} for computing XUX (See Section 3.1).

4.2. Implementing SGSS

It can be observed from the formulas presented in Section 3 that SGSS is a linear combination of several measures, with weights wOS,wOF,wOR,wHR,wSRel,wSF,wCompw_{\mathrm{OS}},w_{\mathrm{OF}},w_{\mathrm{OR}},w_{\mathrm{HR}},w_{\mathrm{SRel}},w_{\mathrm{SF}},w_{\mathrm{Comp}}. Hence, if the SGSS scores of a given pair of summaries from the above dataset are denoted by SGSS​(SLEFT)\textit{SGSS}(S^{\mathrm{LEFT}}) and SGSS​(SRIGHT)\textit{SGSS}(S^{\mathrm{RIGHT}}), the following is also a linear combination of the same measures with the above weights:

(13) Δ​SGSS=SGSS​(SLEFT)−SGSS​(SRIGHT).\Delta\textit{SGSS}=\textit{SGSS}(S^{\mathrm{LEFT}})-\textit{SGSS}(S^{\mathrm{RIGHT}})\ .

Since we have a preference label for each summary pair as well as the absolute labels for the overviews, headings, and statements in the summaries, we can apply (say) logistic regression to the training portion of the dataset to determine the weights, where the target variable is the probability that SLEFTS^{\mathrm{LEFT}} is better than SRIGHTS^{\mathrm{RIGHT}}. This will give us our first instantiation of SGSS.

We will also consider model selection: can we simplify the definition of SGSS by removing one or more evaluation criteria?

4.3. Evaluating SGSS

We would like SGSS to agree with human summary preferences. To check this, we can use the test portion of our dataset (which was not used for tuning the weights), and compute the agreement rate for each summary pair:

(14) AR=#human preference labels that agree with ​Δ​SGSSH.\textit{AR}=\frac{\text{\#human preference labels that agree with }\Delta\textit{SGSS}}{H}\ .

Here, although we have both human and LLM-based labels for the test data, we will have to check whether relying only on LLM-based labels suffices, because we would like to be able to automatically estimate whether a given new summary is better than another. (We will first have to examine the reliability of LLM-based labels by comparing them with the human labels.) We will then take the mean of AR over the summary pairs in the test set to obtain the Mean AR (MAR) (Sakai and Zeng, 2021). We want the MAR of SGSS to be as high as possible.

5. Summary

We proposed a framework for evaluating structured generative search summaries that are placed atop organic web search results, and described our plans for implementing and evaluating the framework. The outcomes of our implementation and evaluation will be reported elsewhere.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
